title: Call of Duty®: Modern Warfare® 4
review_text: Genuinely surprised. Especially by DMZ. It's certainly too early to write a thorough review, but I can confidently say that I'm pleasantly surprised. Far more than I ever expected to be. I'll start with the campaign. I genuinely did not expect it to be this immersive. It's been a long time since a Call of Duty campaign managed to pull me in like this. I'm talking about the days of the original Modern Warfare trilogy. The kind of campaign that stays on your mind long after you've turned off the game, and actually makes you look forward to getting back on. What really caught me off guard was how dark and grounded the story feels. There are moments where you genuinely sit there thinking, "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, did that just happen?" The moral ambiguity, the uncomfortable situations, the realism of certain scenarios... it almost feels disturbingly believable. Like something that could genuinely happen in the real world. I haven't experienced that feeling from a Call of Duty campaign in a very long time. - *Now, DMZ. This is where I was REALLY taken aback.* For context, I've never been particularly interested in Battle Royale, Warzone, or those types of game modes. They just never appealed to me. However, I have spent plenty of time playing extraction shooters like Escape from Tarkov, so I'm familiar with the genre. And somehow, DMZ just hits differently. I honestly can't put my finger on exactly what makes it so satisfying. There's something about the balance they've achieved between exploration, looting, combat, progression, and extraction that just works. It doesn't feel unnecessarily complicated, but it doesn't feel shallow either. There's enough tension to keep you on your toes, enough progression to keep you invested, and enough freedom to make every deployment feel different. The movement feels clean, the gameplay feels fluid, and the overall experience is just genuinely enjoyable. And when you've got a friend or two joining you? It gets even better. I've already sunk over 10 hours into the game (DMZ), and I can comfortably say I'll be sinking plenty more into it. Not because I feel obligated to grind something, but because I'm genuinely having fun. That's something I haven't been able to say about a Call of Duty game in quite some time. Again, these are early impressions, and I'm curious to see how everything develops with the full release. I'm not claiming it's perfect, nor am I pretending I've experienced everything the game has to offer. But credit where credit is due. *The campaign has genuinely impressed me, and DMZ has completely exceeded my expectations.* I came in expecting another Call of Duty. Instead, I've found myself thinking about the game when I'm not even playing it. That's usually a pretty good sign. I Recommended Call of Duty®: Modern Warfare® 4. So far, they've earned it.

And when the community finally gets something like a buff or a decent change its usually only because AH shafted the player base in a major way a minute prior an even when they do say they will buff or change something they usually try and back out of it after getting good press or make changes so unimpactful that everything feels the same. EAC was implemented because in ~2 weeks modders had fixed what arrow head had they they are working on for ~2 YEARS and players were finally able to have fun in the game without all the intentional constant annoyances so in turn they put in EAC and gutted the systems they work on to stop people from modding. review_text: Not a huge fan of the game's direction anymore and I'm extremely worried it'll collapse under its own short term decisions. They're pushing more boring events than ever to waste your time with minimal rewards, usually two pulls worth of currency for doing a full event. Extraction mode is awful, super boring with gated progression away from your characters and they're going full tilt into it locking premium currency behind playing it. We've gone an ENTIRE YEAR without a new A-rank character (for those unaware, it means a free to play friendly character). Manato came out October 2025 and since then it's been a nonstop slew of S-rank (premium) powercreeping goonbait girls with less and less of the sauce that made 1.0's roster so cool. There's two things happening at once - less options for F2P players and way less diversity in character designs. We had a masked power ranger man with guns, a huge bear using a battering ram, a maid with a bloodborne-style saw, a wolf with prosthetic jet engine legs?! It's trended massively towards just girls with huge tits and short skirts now to squeeze dry the most debased section of the playerbase. I have no idea why hoyo is introducing a new element and a new class, it's a crying shame that the defense class is completely unusable in end game content and abandoned in its entirety in favour of "armourer"? I have zero idea where they're going with characters in the future but I guarantee we won't see any more rupture characters, defense or even armourer, it seems pointless that they even added it because it doesn't fill any missing niche. It all feels like short term solutions and gimmicks without considering a wider ecosystem of how you use these classes together. Rupture, for example, is meant to be a high damage class that ignores defence but needs extremely specific supporting characters and has absolutely zero interplay with any other existing systems. We got it and it was meta for a bit, but will gradually be outclassed and powerscaled unless they want to spend 6 months adding a few new S-rank rupture characters out of the blue since there's no A-ranks anymore. 2.0 loved rupture but that'll be gone, it also loved anomaly, which has received nonstop meta characters during that time and up to the current update (3.3). The entire system feels unbalanced and aimless right now where your best bet is just using Anomaly, which in itself requires massive investment in S-rank characters and weapons. To give it credit, I think the game is worth a go to new players to see if you click with it. The animations and art style are top notch still, the QoL they've added over time is welcome and combat is great. These kept me going but I'm quitting while I'm ahead before everything becomes more enshittified.

review_text: DbD is one of those games which you pick up at first, have fun for a little bit, and then set down after a while. The gameplay loop is rather repetitive after about 100 matches or so. The balancing of perks is terrible (Will touch on my experiences with that later in the review), with some of the survivor being absolutely busted compared to their killer counterparts, and the killer role is more of a victim role IMO. New killers to this game, since Springtrap, have been the same thing, 4.4 m/s movement, with a projectile. Because it's almost like the devs cant come up with more innovative ideas. And whenever you go against these killers the strategy is the same, keep your ears and eyes open for any stray projectiles when you go against them. Especially Jason, his notifier is global for some bizarre reason. And the Judgement? Pretty easy to counter, you see the projectile as its coming towards you so you can move out of the way. There was even a suggested balance so that there would be a border around your screen telling you it was coming so you didn't have to pay as much attention to the game as you should be. Updates that are seasonal events are often reused (reduce, reuse, and recycle guys!) content, especially the current Halloween event going on, with that just being a more watered down version of the event with orange juice filter over it. Much worse than its predecessor from over a year ago. The event they replaced the Twisted Masquerade with, the Black Banquet, is for the survivor, grab an item, regenerate a health state, and then also gain immunity, or a speed boost, whilst the killer has nothing but a ball of poison to slow the survivors. Alongside some of the terrible events they have, they also suck at patching legacy bugs, and balancing! Now they did try rebalancing perks in a recent patch, but to no avail. With 90% of the meta perks still being used to this day. The QA team for this game is severely incompetent as they seem to not be able to test correctly, and numerous bugs that should've been patched day 1, still remain in the game years later, with singularities pods not being placed on surfaces that are highlighted, being one of those bugs that has been there for years now. Finally, the community, if you just want to play the game in private matches with your friends, then go for it! You wont have to deal with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ community of this game. But the community is god awful, if you can, avoid at all times interacting with them because you'll end up wanting to end it all. Heres the TL:DR: The Gameplay loop is OK, new killers suck (especially Springtrap and Jason), balancing and new events are recycled, watered down versions of their former selves, and the community is unbearable. Would I have bought the game if I had known what I was getting into? No.

title: Enshrouded
review_text: I don’t write reviews often, but as far as open-world RPG survival crafting games go, this one feels like the logical endpoint and a high peak for the genre. It’s an absolute 10 when it comes to aesthetics, exploration, building, workshops, resources, co-op, and the general sense of adventure. The voxel-based rendering makes the world feel alive and seamless, especially with player-made structures. My friends and I have put hundreds of hours into it, and there’s still plenty of side content left. My one and only complaint is the combat. It’s god-awful. At its best it’s boring and tedious, and at its worst it’s insanely frustrating. I’m talking about melee specifically. As you progress through the skill tree you unlock special moves with unique animations, but the combat is so floaty and weird that these attacks miss about 70% of the time. You lunge, dive, or aerial attack and fly right past the target, whether you’re locked on or not. Most of the special moves end up feeling useless because it’s more effective to just stand in a group of enemies and spin around swinging. Melee combat is simply too floaty. It doesn’t help that a huge number of enemies are tiny insectoids about the height of a pair of running shoes; you swing right over their heads if the ground is even slightly slanted. (Would it have killed them to make robot llamas instead of yet another scorpion variant?) I’ve been playing since day one of early access, and watching this game grow has been a great experience. The latest combat overhaul mostly just added a heavy attack that still misses half the time. I’d love to see the combat system improve as much as the rest of the game has. Make lock-on actually matter, and make it so you at least pivot toward an enemy if they shift slightly while you’re attacking, so it doesn’t feel like you’re wasting your time. All in all, though, it’s still an excellent game. I’m looking forward to seeing where the developers take it—whether that’s more content or even a sequel.

review_text: Enshrouded hits the sweet spot between Valheim’s survival progression and Breath of the Wild’s fluid exploration. The voxel engine is the real standout—you aren't just snapping pre-fab walls together; you can carve a custom base out of a mountain face or meticulously restore ancient ruins brick by brick. The Good Unmatched Building & Terraforming: True voxel-based building gives you total creative freedom without feeling clunky or restrictive. Tense Shroud Mechanics: Diving into fog-filled valleys for rare loot under a countdown timer keeps exploration high-stakes and addictive. Flexible Progression: The radial skill tree allows effortless respecs at any Flame Altar, letting you switch seamlessly between a Battlemage, Ranger, or tank without restarting. Handcrafted Map: Moving away from procedural generation in favor of a massive, handcrafted world with soaring spires and gliding routes pays off immensely. The Bad Early-Game Inventory: Managing resources across five separate artisan NPCs requires tedious sorting until you unlock magic chests. Missing Inventory & Chest Locking: There is currently no option to lock favorited inventory items (risking accidental deposits, salvaging, or sales) nor any native way to lock personal storage chests from other players on co-op servers. Verdict If you enjoy open-world survival, deep building systems, and rewarding exploration, this is an absolute must-play. Easily one of the best survival action RPGs on Steam.

Maybe it will be more fun playing with friends though.

title: Enshrouded
review_text: Almost 30 hours in and I havent even scratched the surface. Me and my wife are absolutely addicted to this game and rush to play this in our freetime and we feel like indulgent teenagers to play this until late in the night. Last time I felt this addicted was V Rising but Enshrouded fixes some things that I had grievances with with V Rising. First and foremost, Im a basebuilder girlie and will spend untold hours prettying up the base and it features SO many decoration possibilities naturally unlocked by exploring. The best part is placing down your base anywhere - even in settlements which you then can treat like a fixer-upper. I play on controller and it takes a tiny bit of time to get used to the decor controls but I think they did a good job mapping them in a way that works once muscle memory kicks in. But being able to place a whopping 12 bases is just so nice because I dont have to decide between aesthetics vs location benefit. The exploration and loot loop is highly addictive. There are ample respawning chests that enable you to liberally scrap stuff for runes for enhancement. My backpack is never big enough, which is usually a good sign to me that there is lots of stuff worth taking - but its not frustrating! With a bit of inventory management with your party, youll be able to spend hours outdoors without having to make hard choices. If you hadnt planned to play this with your friends before, maybe see them as useful extensions to your backpack >:) But location-wise this game scratches ALL the exploration itches. There are a perfect amount of locations to explore, theyre big (or small) enough to feel just the right size and feel very natural in structure, placing and vibe. Gives me the same rush as stumbling over some an area in BotW/TotK or even Dragons Dogma 1/2 but now its co-op and that just makes me SO happy. Combat is pretty nice. Compared to the other features of the game, combat would be the one "weak point" because despite the big skill tree, I dont find it suuuuper diverse, but maybe that also just because Im not using magic or am still super early in (Area 2 of 6). Meanwhile, my wife is having a blast crafting spells and Im all too happy to fuel her mana-induced megalomania. <3 Combat feels like a lite version of dark souls as a STR build, where currently Im just heavy-attacking everything into being stunned and often just smacking stuff until its dead, but at least enemy variation keeps it relatively fresh. Again, magic might make this look totally different, but I dont hate combat, its just not the selling point. Its not bad at all and Ive played plenty of games with worse combat systems! Now my personal highlights were actually something HIGHLY unexpected; the music, atmosphere and lore. I bought this game in EA but I didnt touch it until 1.0 and for some reason didnt expect it to have... lore? At least not this extensive. Totally optional btw, if lore is something that makes you hiss like a vampire. But if youre someone who enjoys high fantasy settings, specifically something that feels like a bleaker version of Elder Scrolls? Yeah. Get this game. While there arent any overworld NPCs (aside from the ones you put in your base), the game has plenty of lore notes, which then also tie into side-quests and do a banger job at tying together worldbuilding, atmosphere and quest details. And the best part? Theyre being read to you by the narrator while youre exploring! Its such a weird little highlight for me to be able to loot while hearing about the lore with good narration (great job @ the voiceactor btw! Its very immersive!). The music is GORGEOUS and conveys mood like nothing else, same with the scenery which is just chefs kiss. We often times just find ourselves soaking in atmosphere, even in the shroud! And the worldbuilding is very solid and cool! I do love myself a well-built world and this very clearly has its own character and vision, and I dig it! Also, worth mentioning is the sheer amount of customization you can do to your game experience. If I would ask for anything more, it would probably be just a small addition in the accessibility settings to be able to disable flashing lights (of which I havent seen many but there are lightning effects) and reduce the white glow/contrast or maybe even disable bloom. While I find the accessibility settings pretty great, We would like to play this with another friend in future, but I cannot see them having an easy time with how brightly everything glows. Other than that, the ability to customize the experience to be easy in some parts and unforgiving in others, is something Ive LOVED. In the end, it was all the polishing and unexpected highlights that to me make this game kind of an insanely hidden gem (dont really know about hidden, but its DEFINITELY a gem) among the open-world survival games. When it all just comes together into a very seamless, smooth and enjoyable experience. I personally love Enshrouded and am pretty certain that after 30 hours I wont fall out of love anytime soon. And please, please, developers. Please make DLC. I dont care if its new areas, Id even buy decoration/furniture packs (in fact, Id kinda go crazy for those heheh). I hope this game sells incredibly well and thank you for making us feel like our indulgent, irresponsible, never-tired teenage-selves again!

review_text: [This review is about multiplayer only.] This game has 2 multiplayer modes. 1. Quick play = Spec racing - every one is equal pretty much. - FINE, but ultimately unfulfilling as you have pretty much bot lobbies or new people every race. 2. Tour Mode = You build your racer over 6 races - RNG mechanics based on where you think you'll finish. (Betting system) - HORRENDOUS. With Quick Play - I demolish 9/10 lobbies. No challenge. There are only so many circuits and shortcuts. 4/6 players are usually bots which is a shame. With Tour Mode - It usually puts you in 1 or 2 races into a 6 tour mode. YOU ARE ALREADY AT A DISADVANTAGE JUST JOINING. The longer the tour goes on, the more the advantage is shifted to the stronger players (You can bet if you end in the top 2 or not, and ending in the top 2 gives you stronger parts for your racer). This wouldn't be so bad if there wasn't such an obviously imbalanced meta - RAMJET. I've had it where I win by over 18 seconds over a 3 lap race. It's insane and ridiculous. You have 3 modes of thrust in order of speed: normal thrust, afterburner, and ramjet. Sometimes the RNG gives you a combo so that it gives you invincible shield using ramjet and infinite cooling using ramjet. Essentially infinite ultimate boost the whole race no matter what even if you crash into walls. Compare this to other RNG where you have great cooldown using afterburner and a boost when you get a jump - you will always lose with the latter even if you know the track inside out and are Anakin Skystappen. There is no skill in multiplayer tour mode. Only RNG. You can know all the shortcuts, be the most skilled player in the lobby, but be overtaken consistently by someone with better RNG than you in their build because of... no reason at all! That's just not how true racing should work in any series. Such a shame as this game has such great visuals, sense of speed and potential. Fuse Games has chosen the Dark Side and you MUST NOT side with them. Losing RNG leads to frustration. Frustration leads to hate. Hate... leads to... suffering. Buy not this game until balanced, you will. [Singeplayer obviously has stupid dumb scripted AI that'll overtake you no matter what until the last lap of the race letting you *feel* like you "won" no matter how fast or slow you go.] EDIT: The latest game updates have made the game unstable too. Game crashes, disconnects, etc. Game was SO STABLE on release. Such a shame.

New content consists of throwing anything at the wall, regardless of how far from the game it is (Duviri takes you from a high-paced sci-fi looter-horde shooter to what I can only describe as subpar dark souls kingdom) or how obviously badly designed it is (Archimedea mixes a randomly generated gear whitelist, which is already incompatible with with a game all about bringing what you want, with randomly chosen modifiers that can singlehandedly cripple large groups of gear. How did this get past the drawing board?). Power creep runs rampant and players have long since become impossible to counter, and instead of dialing it back or at least keeping things as stable as they can get, we get entirely new problems, with modes that try to counter us anyway (and inevitably become a slog that people take the path of least resistance through) and abilities that tamper with the most basic mechanics (Cyte-09 has X-ray and wall penetration, follie can spawn gamemode items on demand). Two, the plot. I'd argue it's been at least a bit messy since duviri, but ever since the old peace, the writing has very quickly gotten very bad. Spectacle and cheap emotions over anything coherent, jumping from scene to scene, consistency be damned, even writing off characters in the cheapest ways possible if they'd get in the way. But look at all the voice actors we've got! Jade shadows constellations is an especially egregious example, and from what was shown off at tennocon, tau doesn't seem like it'll be an exception. As I write this, there's also an event that makes the same mistake destiny's seasons made: putting main story beats behind deliberately ephemeral content, which in this case is explicitly advertised as not returning for good measure. If we don't get anything to fill in for it when it ends, that'll be a proper destiny moment. Three, extremely short-sighted design decisions, ham-fisted balance changes, and horrific (if any) handling of feedback pertaining to those. Far too many times has this scenario played out: Something gets announced. People immediately call out glaring issues. With very few exceptions, nothing changes by launch, with little to no acknowledgement of the feedback at any point. I can think of at least 8 things this has happened to. Overguard, archimedea, the aerial melee slam nerf, valkyr's rework, tauron strikes, arcane persistence, follie's hunt, vauban's minelayer rework, most recently ammo efficiency on riven mods. Valkyr's the one case I can think of where something did come of the feedback. After some... to say the least, bizarre changes before launch and IIRC 3 months of dead silence, someone got told 'Valkyr rework is great and you are wrong' and that was that. I can only recommend this if you really like the core gameplay but can also put up with the game trying to take it away at every opportunity and the team's apparent lack of passion for the game. Which I can't imagine is a very common sentiment.

title: WARDOGS
review_text: ⭐ 0/10 — WAR DOGS: A LOVE LETTER TO EVERYTHING THAT CAN GO WRONG Congratulations to War Dogs, the only game I've played where I can spend 20 minutes trying to enjoy myself and somehow come away feeling like I've just completed a mandatory workplace safety seminar. This game is what happens when Battlefield, Call of Duty, and a bowl of expired spaghetti get thrown into a blender operated by someone who's never played a video game before. Let's start with the movement. Moving around in War Dogs feels like you're controlling a refrigerator full of wet cement. Every step feels like a legal dispute between your character's legs and the ground. Trying to navigate basic terrain is less like being an elite soldier and more like watching a drunk shopping cart attempt to escape a Walmart parking lot. And the gunplay? Absolutely magnificent. Nothing makes you feel like a highly trained operator quite like shooting someone and wondering whether your bullets actually exist. Sometimes you're convinced you've landed enough shots to qualify as a war crime, only to discover that your enemy apparently has the structural integrity of a nuclear bunker. Meanwhile, you get looked at funny from three counties away and immediately return to the main menu. The vehicles deserve their own criminal investigation. Driving feels like every vehicle was assembled from spare parts found at a scrapyard after a natural disaster. And the helicopters? Oh, the helicopters. Flying one feels like trying to balance a washing machine on top of a ceiling fan during an earthquake. You don't pilot an aircraft; you negotiate with gravity and hope it accepts your terms. Then there's the optimization. My computer can apparently render an entire battlefield, calculate complex physics, and run dozens of applications simultaneously, but War Dogs occasionally behaves like displaying a tree is an unsolved mathematical problem. Nothing says immersion like your game turning into a slideshow at the exact moment someone decides to introduce you to their entire ammunition supply. The sound design is another masterpiece of confusion. Sometimes you hear footsteps. Sometimes you hear gunfire. Sometimes you hear absolutely nothing until you're suddenly staring at a death screen wondering whether the enemy arrived by teleportation, wormhole, or a premium subscription to the audio system. And let's talk about the UI and overall polish. The game has the distinct energy of a group project where one person did all the work, three people disappeared, and the last person submitted the assignment at 11:59 PM with half the instructions missing. Menus, mechanics, and general usability can feel like they're daring you to discover how much patience you actually have. The balance is equally entertaining. Every match feels like a social experiment designed to determine how long human beings can tolerate being inconvenienced before they begin questioning their life choices. You don't always feel outplayed. Sometimes you feel like you lost a fight against the game's questionable decisions. And the progression? Nothing quite says fun like grinding through an experience that occasionally makes you wonder whether you're being rewarded for playing well or simply compensated for enduring the suffering. Every unlock feels less like an achievement and more like receiving a certificate for surviving another shift at a job you hate. The worst part is that there's probably a decent game buried somewhere underneath all this nonsense. The concept has potential. The large-scale combat can be entertaining. There are moments where you catch a glimpse of what the game could become. Then the game reminds you what it currently is. War Dogs is like buying a brand-new car, discovering the steering wheel is optional, the brakes work on a subscription basis, the radio only plays static, and the dealership tells you that the experience is part of the charm. I genuinely want to enjoy this game. I want to jump into a match, have a great time, and walk away thinking, "Damn, that was awesome." Instead, I walk away thinking, "Damn, I should've just stared at my desktop for an hour." FINAL VERDICT: 0/10 — WOULD RATHER BE COURT-MARTIALED. War Dogs isn't necessarily the worst game ever made. That would imply it has achieved a level of failure worthy of historical recognition. No, War Dogs is something far more frustrating: a game with enough potential to keep you playing, enough problems to make you regret it, and just enough good moments to convince you that maybe, just maybe, the next match won't be an absolute clown fiesta. And then the next match starts. God help us all. P.S. If the developers ever fix everything wrong with this game, I'll happily come back and update this review. Until then, I'm fairly certain my character, my helicopter, and my remaining brain cells are all eligible for veteran benefits.

title: We Were Here Tomorrow
review_text: I love this series and was really looking forward to the new installation (bought it immediately). I was quite surprised by the number of negative reviews because I played the demo and didn’t notice anything terrible there; on the contrary, I was really drawn to the visuals (each new part looks better and better). I should note right away that we haven't used the in-game voice chat since the very first games, because we play in the same room sitting back-to-back. However, I understand that a broken chat can be a major issue for many, though in that case, I would just use Discord or at least wait for hotfixes. Buying the game now is a great value anyway, and it's a good way to support the developers—a lack of built-in chat doesn't make the game itself bad. After playing for 7 hours, I can safely say that the puzzles haven't gotten any worse. They've never been overly difficult, but they've always been highly collaborative. The idea of ​​adding unique character abilities was a great touch, as it allowed the devs to introduce new puzzles and teamwork without forcing players to stay separated for the entire game. Personally, I prefer dark fantasy over sci-fi, but I still really dig the style, especially considering how much they expanded the lore by introducing the rifts. On top of that, the environmental storytelling is excellent (the way lore is told through objects, the density of the world, and the genuine feeling that people actually lived and worked in these rooms). As for motion sickness, I am exactly the kind of person who gets motion sick even in vehicles (which is why I absolutely hate it when games don't have a setting to turn off head bobbing, especially when it serves no gameplay purpose). However, I didn't experience any issues with this game, because the moments with rotations and spatial distortions were brief and strictly tied to gameplay mechanics. review_text: It's such a smooth playing game. The added bits of movement and fluidity of it made almost every combat encounter the most engaged I feel i've ever been on a normal difficulty Gears campaign. I didn't notice it in the early hours, but once the full enemy suite arrives and the mid to late game combat encounters ramp up, they will be your biggest opponent. If you go down, it always takes them a handful of seconds to even react and pick you up, even if you were downed right next to them, or they'll straight up run away from you. If you're able to play with someone or even a full group, this will be a non issue, especially with the ability in the game to change up loadouts and equipment. The other weak aspect is are the couple of open ended sections. The first one in the second hour of the game isn't so bad, but the next later in just made me continue on with the story. I personally dont like these open map sections. Some positives. The opening is great. Having that confusion brought upon by E-Day led to this rushed and frantic feel in the beginning and the Locust felt just as horrific as they felt in the original game. All the new weapons feel great to use and have their utility. The graphics are top notch and there were multiple moments, both in the beauty and the horrific that made me stop and stare for a bit. This is just about the campaign, I dont know how much, if any of the multiplayer i'll jump into, but I will for sure be partaking in horde as it was the mode 18 years ago that sucked up a lot of my free time.

title: MapleStory
review_text: I'm reviewing Classic I've played Maplestory as my main mmorpg, off and on since Ludibrium was first added. Over the years I've wanted something like a classic version of this game that isn't a private server, and finally we have one. First impressions are that it looks and feels like Maplestory as it was pre-Big Bang. It was refreshing. The leveling curve was as grindy as I remembered, and all the old places and spots were as they were. The game was stripped of most of the bloat that the main game currently has. I did notice some changes that I didn't expect like new skills, new level requirements, and new ways to fuel the in-game economy that wasn't introduced in the game back then. Most of my experience has been positive, however my current issues with the game are the current limitations. Maple has never made it easy to boost ones in-game financial stability in the early days, and this part of the game has revealed itself again. You are almost dedicated to the market as much as you are to grinding and leveling up. Not to mention that the current state of the in-game economy (and RL tbf) is unstable and fluctuating daily, and it feels like spending is thin among the general population yet there's shops everywhere, and not enough shop space in the Free Market on ALL channels. Again, you would have to commit to the market and use up a lot of time that could be used elsewhere. Also, the need to fill ones own pocket almost requires you spend money in order to do so. TLDR: The game is great if you are going in for nostalgia or to experience the greatness of the early days of Maplestory, but it is tough for anyone new and unwilling to spend actual money. I am hopeful since I am only playing the founders early access version, that the game will open up when F2P arrives, and that more will be added to stabilize the game.

title: Fallout 76
review_text: Bethesda and ZeniMax Media: Two Sides of the Same Coin Stay away from this company if you value your dignity and time. They banned my ESO account, into which I invested thousands of hours and money, based on false cheating accusations. Their support tickets provide no meaningful answers or evidence. They refer only to messages I exchanged with another player, interpreting “want to farm money?” as a reference to cheating. That is their justification. I have never experienced such unprofessionalism despite having played many games. At this point, there is no forgiveness for either of you. I recently got into this game and discovered what I had gotten myself into: “ZeniMax Media Terms of Service.” I'm seriously frustrated, and it is already too late to request a refund. Honest Overall Review 1. Company and Trust This company is dishonest, deceitful, and unprofessional. I say this clearly and without exaggeration. Evidence and recent reports can be found across well-known platforms. 2. Bugs and Unresolved Issues Many bugs have existed for years without being fixed. Here are some examples. 2.1. Stationary Enemies and Possible Exploits After an hour, I noticed that mobs in many houses stood completely still, even after detecting or attacking them. This allows players to farm XP without any challenge. I first noticed this inside a house near the northern or northeastern entrance to Whitespring Resort. I exploited the possible bug by luring mobs towards the door, making them return inside with reduced HP from my shots. Feel free to ban me for that! 2.2. Completely Bugged Main Quest "Thicker Than Water" This quest lets you kill Frankie or save him. If you choose to kill him, Beckett never fires his weapon, preventing completion. I replayed it six or seven times, trying different approaches and spending around ten minutes per attempt. Beckett simply stared at Frankie, and nothing happened. YouTube videos showed both players who successfully completed this choice and others experiencing the same bug. Reports dating back years suggest it remains unresolved. Against my wishes, I eventually saved Frankie and completed the quest without problems. 2.3. “Disconnected from Server” After an Update After a recent update, I started receiving “disconnected from server” when entering a server. I don't know whether it is connected to my banned ESO account or simply another bug. Online reports suggest resolution can take weeks. Given this company's policies, I fear another unjustified ban, even across different games. We buy games only to risk being banned without justification or evidence. I submitted a ticket because the servers appeared online and functional. This was when I discovered that ZeniMax is the “mother” behind this entire mess. 3. Customer Support My trust in this company is 0%. Search for “Fallout 76 bugs” and filter recent results to find countless unresolved issues. I encountered several myself but managed to work around them without seriously affecting gameplay. Gameplay 1. Difficulty, Progression, and Farming This is an easy game. I reached level 60 and learned around 90% of its content, including builds, trading, mutations, farming, and events. Some may find it complex, but I found it simple once I learned how everything worked, one thing at a time. The farming system is poor, especially for plants. They respawn based on how many other items you collect, not simply with time. You may need to collect around 1,000 other items before the original ones respawn. This is strange, confusing, and ridiculous. The beginning can be confusing because the game explains things poorly, but after several hours, you learn practically everything. 2. Missions and Group Activities Group missions are limited, extremely repetitive, sometimes slow, and generally too easy. I haven't tried every game mode, but a quick search will show you what to expect. 3. Inventory Management and Incentives to Spend Money Limited inventory space seems designed to encourage purchases. You must carefully manage your inventory and keep only essential items, spending considerable time doing so. Gameplay: Combat, AI, and Menus Combat “V.A.T.S.” is essentially an auto-aim mechanic against enemies, making it excellent for players with ping issues. Official servers are another advantage, particularly for players with Strict NAT connections. However, daily maintenance can take several hours. Artificial Intelligence (AI) The enemy AI is average. I cannot call it terrible, but it certainly isn't good either. Menus and Interface The menus are peculiar and interesting, but the experience is terrible. They are disorganized, difficult to manage, and lack decent filters. Inventory and quick-menu management waste time on tasks that should be simple. The game feels almost prehistoric in this regard. Assigning an item to the quick menu, such as key 3, can take almost a minute because finding it is so cumbersome. The favorites system helps little; the experience remains prehistoric. In-Game Market I would give it 4/10. It works, but I would not give it 5/10. Positive Points 1. Pay-to-Win (P2W) and Paid Advantages I couldn't determine with 100% certainty whether the game is P2W, but I am almost certain it isn't. The game encourages subscriptions for inventory benefits and other advantages. I managed my inventory by prioritizing damage and defense over perks or cards that reduce item weight or increase capacity. These perks make inventory management easier but reduce combat efficiency, especially when playing solo, as I do. 2. Busy Servers and Finding Groups Easily The servers are populated, and finding groups is easy. However, there is no in-game text chat, which is a downside, although voice chat is available. 3. Progression and Boss Difficulty Certain bosses can challenge beginners, but a decent weapon, such as a Gatling Gun, and safe positioning make combat extremely easy. Even with an average or poor build, defeating them is possible. Enemies with no stars or one or two stars require a good weapon, even without mods. With mods, you can eventually take on three- and four-star bosses solo. I never experienced a genuine feeling of difficulty. Leaving this game is therefore the best option for me. 4. Environment and Scenery The environment is beautiful. The variety of biomes and changing weather make the game more interesting. 5. Community The players I encountered, solo or in public groups, generally provided a positive experience. When someone gives you an item, it is usually because they no longer need it or consider it junk. Later, you will also leave many items behind. At first, however, they seem valuable because you have little equipment or do not yet understand the importance of inventory management. The game has a more mature player base. I hope they eventually break free from this addiction and stop supporting a company that deserves nothing but complete rejection. Summary and Ratings Performance, Stability and Servers: 8/10 Fun: 6/10 AI and Gameplay (Combat): 5/10 Story: I did not pay enough attention to evaluate it. P2W?: 7/10 - It does not seem pay-to-win, but I am not 100% certain. Trust in Bethesda/ZeniMax: 1/10 Bugs: 7/10 - Many remain unresolved for years. My worst experience was a main quest offering two choices, one of which did not work, forcing me to restart and choose the only option that allowed completion. Customer Support (Overall): 1/10 Overall Rating: 2/10 I thank the people responsible for this game for showing me “disconnected from server.” Without it, I might still have been tempted to spend money on a company that does not deserve my respect.

review_text: So it's culturally, it's the 1950's, tech has advanced unusually high but this doesn't stop your neighborhood retaining that old-timey slice of America feel. Then the bombs went off! Enter Vault Tech, who crafted that happy-go-lucky dystopian society underground, except it's now Reclamation Day which means it's time to return to the surface! But don't worry! You're given some handy tools (by Mister Handy no less) before you're given the boot out of the Vault, but will that be enough to not just survive, but thrive? I waited till this game had been out a couple years before I gave it a chance. I'm glad I finally did. West Virginia has never looked more beautiful or dystopian in this campy romp for survival. review_text: Okay so I downloaded this game on August 1st for ONE reason: Jingran. Saw him once and decided I'm installing a whole gacha game for him. Zero regrets. He's my main, he's getting his full resonance chain on his rerun, and I'm so glad I finally got the game. What I didn't expect was to fall this hard for everything else. The story is genuinely GOOD. I'm the person who refuses to skip dialogue, and this game rewards that. Mengzhou's arc had me emotionally invested in ways I was not prepared for, and the cutscenes are gorgeous. The music too is so well done. Combat feels SO good once it clicks. Swapping characters, Outro/Intro combos, landing a clean rotation, it's satisfying in a way that makes you want to keep building your team. The echo system is a whole rabbit hole too. Is it RNG pain sometimes? Absolutely, I once had seven bad rolls in a row. But when you finally hit that perfect substat on your last try? Best feeling in the world. The gacha is fair as these things go. You can lose 50/50s (ask me how I know), but the weapon banner is a guaranteed featured 5-star at pity, there's no 50/50 for weapons, and the game is generous enough that you can save up and actually plan your pulls. but.... a 50/50 pity system like the one in Genshin called Capturing Radiance would be so nice... because I have lost 4 50/50s and have yet to win one in this game. Exploration is fun,(I spend lots of time just looking for chests and minigames) the world is beautiful, and the characters are designed with so much love. review_text: Great Potential Undermined by Progression Bugs and Unaccountable Customer Support** Aniimo has the potential to be an enjoyable game, but my experience with its progression systems and customer support has raised serious concerns. The biggest problem isn't simply that bugs exist. Bugs happen in games. *he problem is what happens when those bugs prevent progression, consume limited opportunities, and the support system fails to meaningfully address them. In Egg Heist's Chaos Mode, players have limited daily attempts, and the mode is essential for progressing toward Emperor rank. When bugs interfere with those attempts, players can lose opportunities they cannot simply recover by playing more. I've encountered reproducible problems that took me approximately 15 minutes to replicate across multiple days. Yet my interactions with support have repeatedly resulted in troubleshooting loops rather than meaningful investigation. Even more concerning is the apparent automation of customer support, where repetitive responses and ticket closures can leave players without an actual resolution or effective escalation path. Players should not be expected to perform a development team's debugging responsibilities just to have a reported issue taken seriously. And when bugs affect limited-time progression, requests for restoring lost opportunities or providing appropriate compensation should not simply go unanswered. I have no issue with developers using AI or automation to improve customer support. I have an issue when the resulting system appears to prioritize closing tickets over resolving complaints. A closed support ticket is not a fixed bug. A generic response is not an investigation. And a player losing progression to a technical failure is not an acceptable substitute for proper quality assurance. I want Aniimo to succeed, but that requires more than interesting gameplay and monetized content. It requires reliable systems, responsive technical support, and respect for players' time. review_text: What can i say? I went into this game with high hopes, but being cautiously aware that this could be just another game that promises a lot and then turns out to be SUPER money hungry. I was genuinely happy when i found out i can do pretty much the ENNTIRE game without ever spending a dime (for full disclosure i have spent a few dollars, more on that in a bit*.) Overall, i really like this game, as evidenced by my time in it LOL. I hope to see more out of this game and hope it never loses it's spirit and general openness of play for those with little to no money to spend. review_text: So far I've had a lot of fun with this game. It has the same vibe of catching monsters as Palworld, but feels more like an MMORPG and a mobile game than a survival crafting one. However, it has a few issues too. The gameplay is fun, love the ability to twine with your Aniimo. The combat feels well thought out, and performs well on both the PC and mobile. Gameplay loops like crafting, obtaining items and so on are also well implemented and I feel like I am progressing constantly. Exploration is fun and reminds me of modern Zelda titles. Lots of puzzles, challenges and mysteries instead of the grind-down quests of the old MMORPG's, which is both fresh and makes the game really fun. The lore is interesting, aside from the main quest which just revolves way too much around the theme, which is perfumes and colors. While the theme is mostly targeted for female audience, and I come from outside of that audience, this is not the issue, but that the dialogue just keeps bringing it up like I had dementia. On the other hand, I have greatly enjoyed helping the little Jawlings and Helmuts become friends and a bunch of other lore outside of the main quest. Graphics look good, but all the human characters kind of look the same even though the character creation is quite detailed. It's just the visual style of the game that feels somewhat lazy in those regards, though the cosmetic options help out quite a bit with that. That being said, I think the graphic requirements can be quite high. The sound then... oh boy. While all the voice acting is fine, environment sounds and the Aniimo are great, the music is like someone poured anime syrup in your ear. There is probably an audience for that, but I think most people will choose to turn the music off like I did. It's just a bit too much. The UI and the in-game store though, big oof. It's what you expect from gacha and mobile games, lots of different currencies, reward tabs, a two-tier battle pass, an optional monthly subscription (doesn't charge you monthly, you buy it for a month with the in-game currency so that's a plus), cosmetics, and consumable items. This is a game that will drain your wallet if you let it. The good side is that progression isn't limited by these things so f2p is still a viable way to play the game, though I'd advice you to conserve the most rare resources like Sparkling Cubes. Overall I'm a big fan of this game and definitely recommend it if you like monster capture games, especially the girly girls (or girly guys) out there will probably enjoy this a great deal, because there's so much cuteness and those kinds of themes, while the game also has a lot to offer to guys like me too. It's a solid 8/10 title and it's got me hooked.

review_text: Now I haven't fully experienced the game yet so I will change my review as time goes on, but so far after an hour playing this game is definitely living up to expectations. I loved the demo and immediately wishlisted and was keeping a close eye on this game in hopes of getting it when it releases. When I was waiting for the final moments until release I was excited and honestly seeing the £15 price did end up making me a little hesitant as I figured an early access game shouldn't really be anything over £10 unless it's already very far along and is already in bug-free form. Nevertheless, I've been itching for a good boxing game in a while and I figured why not and splashed the £15 on the game. Least to say I thoroughly enjoyed. I started out in the career mode and made my own guy now one thing I was a little disappointed in here is you don't get to choose a starting weight and have your division to stick within to my knowledge it just defaults you to 200lb area not sure if maybe height pre-determines the weight or anything I'd have to check on another slot. Either way this was my only criticism at that stage I was a bit gutted by the lack of customisation on weight and then moved on. Not sure if you get to bounce between any weight classes as a pro and a little confused with the champion stuff as I'm still an amateur so I'm hoping once I go pro it shifts me somewhere else rather than this being a natural progression thing where you have to go pro at a certain rank to move up. Now when the tutorial started I did feel a little overwhelmed with just how many different things you've got, but the tutorial did help and once I'd had my first 2 fights I'd gotten into the swing of things. The range of things you can do and keep in mind I've only played for an hour so I've not scratched the surface of doing any of the casino or mob stuff yet but the job minigames are great I love the woodcutting one feels smooth and once you get the hang of it just plays great. Same with the training minigames big on the heavy bag one having to get it where the line tells you to overall just amazing. Now onto the bread and butter here the fight week and the fighting itself. I like the fight weeks although I wish you'd have choice over your opponents once again not sure if you get that once you go pro and I'll update once I have on any of this stuff. I like how you need to make weight though and you have that day before weigh-in. Although I'd like to point out another issue I kinda have here. As much as I do like the weight system I feel like it forces you to stick within these lines and if you gain over the weight when you've already made weight and eat on fight day it just makes you fat and slow. I'd prefer if there was a trade-off with it where you don't just instantly become fat, but you become slower but now hit harder where there's benefits to gaining weight on fight day, but not without consequences. Finally my favourite part the fighting. I love the fighting and for a 2D game these guys need to be commended for the incredible job they've done. Feels like there's far more to it than even a game like Undisputed and I can see myself getting absorbed in this a whole lot more because of the fight mechanics. The only issue I'd like to point out with fighting is the predicted scorecards serve to be kind of a useless feature. I know the main point is to gauge whether you're up or not so you know what to do for the next round, but it doesn't actually seem to work. Outside of KD rounds in my experience every single round on the predicted scorecards goes 10-9 to the other guy. This happens even when I KO the guy to find out that same round was scored in my favour by the judges. I'm not sure if maybe it just considers a different category to judges as in some of these rounds I was outlanded, but I had hurt the other guy and was on the verge of dropping him so maybe the judges consider that but predicted scorecards don't? Not entirely sure it's not a huge complaint just something I find a little confusing. Overall, in my experience so far I HIGHLY recommend this game if you're a person who loves career mode as this game delivers undoubtedly the deepest career mode I've ever seen in any game ever hands down. It's got real variety in it and I'm still yet to uncover the whole thing so it'll only get better from here. I hope the devs continue with this game as it's exceptional and I will be playing with each update to come. Don't dismiss it for the 2D art nor the price as deceiving as they can be this game is a gem and well worth the price.

title: Bruisers 2D Boxing
review_text: Easily my favourite boxing game ever. Bruisers is full of charm and personality, but don’t let the pixel art fool you. Under the hood there’s a properly deep boxing simulation. Stamina, heart rate, cuts and injuries all matter. You have to manage your energy, pick your shots and work the body. Between rounds you’re patching up cuts in your corner. The top-level CPU fighters learn your habits as the fight goes on, so you can’t win with the same trick all night. Away from the ring, the career mode is packed with character. You train through minigames, take odd jobs to pay the bills, deal with your entourage, and fight your way up the rankings. You also deal with the seedy underbelly of the boxing world too, with PED's, gear altering, illegal betting on the dark net and more. The graphics, sound and music take me straight back to being a kid, playing 16-bit games on the sofa with a mate. Local two-player is a riot, and it’s exactly that feeling. I was disappointed when the release date was pushed back. After almost 80 hours of the Early Access release, I can confidently say the delay was well worth it. It’s been improved in every way. Highly recommended. Don’t miss out.

It’s the perfect “just one more thing” game that somehow turns into an entire evening of peaceful Disney joy. If you love cozy games, Disney, or simply want a world that feels warm and inviting, Disney Dreamlight Valley is an absolute must-play. Five stars, no question—this one lives on my console permanently.

title: ARC Raiders
review_text: First of all, I'd like to thank the developers for this amazing game! I've put over 150 hours into it, and I've genuinely enjoyed my time playing, especially when the PvE game mode was available. Playing it with my friends was a lot of fun, and it really showed how enjoyable the game can be when cooperation is encouraged. Unfortunately, since that mode was removed, the PvPvE experience has started to feel like nothing more than pure, hardcore PvP. It feels more like a battle royale than a game where PvP and PvE are supposed to coexist. Every time raiders encounter each other, it seems like the only option is to shoot on sight, with no attempt at cooperation whatsoever. It's becoming increasingly frustrating for players who simply want to explore, take down ARC enemies, and enjoy the PvE side of the game. You can barely go anywhere without someone sneaking up behind you and shooting you just to steal your loot. Out of eight raids where I went in without a weapon, I was killed by other players in all eight of them. Some even laughed at me before finishing me off. The biggest issue, in my opinion, is that this mentality is going to ruin cooperative encounters and major PvE events. Missions involving the Frigate, Matriarch, Queen, and other challenging ARC encounters are supposed to encourage players to work together, or at least give them a common objective. But if everyone is too busy trying to kill other raiders before even reaching the objective, how are these encounters supposed to remain enjoyable or even realistically achievable? I'm not saying that PvP should be removed entirely. I understand that it's part of what makes the game unique. However, there needs to be a better balance between PvP and PvE. Right now, it feels like PvP is overshadowing everything else, leaving very little room for cooperation or peaceful encounters. In my opinion, bringing back a dedicated PvE mode and significantly increasing the difficulty of ARC enemies would be a good step towards restoring that balance. This would give players who enjoy PvE a place to play the game the way they want, while making PvE encounters more challenging and rewarding for those who prefer the PvPvE experience. The game has so much potential, and I genuinely want to see it succeed. I just hope the developers will consider how important the balance between PvP, PvE, and cooperation is to the long-term health of the game. Thanks for taking the time to read this, and thank you again for creating such a great game!

title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse
review_text: Belmont's Curse is absolute fire! This game is a big celebration of Castlevania's 40th anniversary! You quickly understand that it was made by fans for fans. It also serves as a great introduction for new fans! First up the gameplay is a lot more platforming action. What I mean is that there are a lot of platforming challenges that range from simple to hard and boy are they difficult but after a few tries you'll get the hang of them. I personally loved them! And when it comes to the action it's a lot more dynamic and dare I say acrobatic. Seriously once you get the two major core abilities that being the Arcane Whip and the Holy Light parry shield, combat flows so nicely. Traversal too and when you get the later abilities, you enter a flow state of pure bliss. Oh and the bosses? Omg they are so fun and so diverse. I really do prefer these more dynamic and almost cinematic boss battles. I hope they add some boss rush mode, I want to do boss rematches! The Arcana are also a very fun idea. I enjoyed completing the challenges to unlock upgrades for their abilities. They are all so varied and never felt useless (except for the starting spell but that gets better later on). This may be unpopular but honestly, I enjoyed the more streamlined RPG mechanics. I enjoyed having weapon families and being able to use whatever I wanted. The relic system while more "barebones" compared to the equipment/abilities from past games, are neat and there's many fun combinations to be had with them but counterpoint, a lot of them are very gimmicky and niche. You probably will discard them in favor of much better ones. The maps you get are all incredibly fun to explore and find secrets and there are so many secrets to find. It also helps how visually pleasing this game is. All the maps and their rooms feel distinct from one another. There are so many fun details and references throughout. Like I mentioned this game is a phenomenal tribute to the Castlevania series! I will say though that the Hall of Mirrors area was a fun challenge to go through but I disliked that distortion effect that lingers throughout. It kind of ruined the exploration for me as I sometimes would get lost and confused. Now it's not all sunshine and rainbows in the gameplay department. I do agree that the Arcane Whip and using healing potions could be a bit faster but for the most part you get used to it. What about the story? Well unlike previous games we get a big focus on the story and characters here. Good. I really love Castlevania's stories and lore and I am so glad we get to experience a cohesive story and plenty of character development and interaction. Rose is a fantastic addition to the Belmont family and seeing her go through some pretty swekl character development and learning from her mistakes is great! I also really enjoyed the interactions that occur between the Fallen, Joan of Arc and Medusa. It almost feels like they plus Rose are meant to be stand-ins for the Castlevania III cast. I'm going to miss them! Lastly, in terms of the art direction and music. It's all pretty darn good. I love the character designs. They all range from cool, badass, elegant and sexy. Top notch stuff. Joan, Medusa, Isaac, Carmilla and Dracula are among my favourites of the designs. The music is good too. No, it doesn't compare to tracks from past games. Belmont's Curse OST is great when you are playing the game. They are more ambient tracks that perfectly fit the area you are in and not once overstay they are welcome, partially because they are longer tracks and so don't loop so early. The use of techno and more R&B tunes work great with all the familiar gothic sounds, choirs and organs of past music tracks, much to the dismay of many "fans". I highly recommend this game. Castlevania is back and we can't let the series go on hiatus again! This is the devs Samus Return, now we need their Dread! Castlevania 1999 anyone? 👀

title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse
review_text: "So when does the game actually start?" is a question I had constantly as I played. The entire game feels like a prologue where you're on a guided tour rather than let loose to explore. And when you DO get to run around on your own it just isn't fun. It's either a tight combat challenge or the most intense parkour of your life, there is no in-between. Even at the end of the game, with all your abilities unlocked and maxed out, Rose feels very clunky and awkward to play. Your movements are slow, your whip never reaches far enough, and the relics are atrocious. You have three relic slots for the entire game, and the relics you can pick vary from "deal 25% more damage in the air" to "run 35% faster if it's a Tuesday and slightly cloudy". The requirements on some relics make them pointless to use, especially when there are SO MANY to collect and 95% of them are useless. The only worthwhile collectables are the final upgrades for every weapon type, because those are where the actual fun is. They change how the weapon behaves and it made me want to collect them all just to see what each weapon could do. But all the tiers below them? Pointless. Some weapon types are so difficult to use (hi twin swords) against the enemies and their behaviour that you're better off ignoring them, finding the final tier, and THEN using them. I enjoyed the tarot card system, acquiring new spells and then performing challenges to unlock extra effects for said spells, but when the only positives are FINAL weapon upgrades and boss rewards, it leaves the rest of the game sorely lacking. Combat is clunky and awkward. Rose is glued to the ground for every attack, her dodge is WAY too short, and enemies are fast, move rapidly, and some can be dodged through while others can't with no discernible difference between the two. You WILL die through no fault of your own repeatedly. And despite the size of the game, the world feels so... small? The castle itself has a main hall, library and clock tower. That's it. I was expecting a lot of unique areas, not three larger zones with a single music track each. Speaking of music: Bloody Tears is a classic, but aside from that one track the rest of the music feels neutered. It genuinely feels likes the music needs a few more layers and audio mixing to really make it pop, because as it stands it's rather forgettable background music. At the end of my playthrough I have to be honest: I didn't have fun. title: RuneScape: Dragonwilds
review_text: Wasn’t sure I’d enjoy it, but I was very wrong! As a long-time OSRS player, I was initially quite unsure about Dragonwilds. I’ve never really been interested in survival games or base building, so I wasn’t convinced this would be for me. Well, I bought it, jumped in with a friend, and ended up playing for four hours on our first night. Safe to say, I absolutely loved it! The game manages to capture a lot of that familiar RuneScape feeling while offering something completely different. The skilling and progression feel rewarding, and even the base building, which I thought I’d dislike, has actually been enjoyable. One thing I’d definitely recommend is playing with a friend. There’s naturally a fair bit of grinding involved, but it’s RuneScape, so that’s hardly a surprise! Progression starts off fairly quick and gradually slows down, exactly as you’d expect. I don’t mind that at all, but having someone alongside you makes gathering resources, levelling skills and exploring much more enjoyable. It really helps break up the grind. The random dragon attacks are another brilliant touch. They keep you on your toes and make the world feel dangerous and unpredictable. Just when you’re getting comfortable doing your own thing, a dragon turns up to remind you that you’re not entirely safe! A few things I’d love to see added in future updates: * Dragon Dagger (DDS) – One of my favourite OSRS weapons. I’d love to see its iconic double-hit special attack and poison damage make their way into Dragonwilds. * Dragon Longsword – Another classic, ideally with its Cleave special attack. * More Scimitars – It’s great seeing familiar weapons like the Rune and Dragon Scimitars, but I’d love the full classic range eventually. I really like the existing special attack system, and I think bringing more of those iconic OSRS weapon abilities into Dragonwilds would be fantastic. Overall, I’m genuinely impressed. I went in expecting that I might not enjoy it, and instead found myself not wanting to log off. If you’re an OSRS player who’s on the fence like I was, I’d definitely recommend giving it a go, especially if you can convince a friend to join you. Really looking forward to seeing how the game develops. Keep up the good work, Jagex!

title: Magic: The Gathering Arena
review_text: TL;DR: Magic: The Gathering Arena is the most generous, fun, and accessible digital card game for casual players—easily beating Hearthstone’s brutal economy and Yu-Gi-Oh’s endless combo turns, despite minor display bugs on ultrawide monitors. A Casual Player’s Perspective on MTG Arena I’m not entirely sure how many total hours I’ve put into MTG Arena between Steam and mobile, but I’d estimate around 30 to 40 hours. For context, I come from a solid card game background: around 300 hours in Hearthstone, roughly 50 hours in modern Yu-Gi-Oh!, and over 300 hours as a legacy Yu-Gi-Oh! player. I originally ran a purely free-to-play account before starting fresh with a new account where I’ve spent maybe $20 to $30 total over the years. I mostly play on my phone, so keep in mind: I’m a casual mobile player who rarely spends money. Here is my honest experience. Economy and Progression: Genuinely Free-to-Play Friendly When I first started years ago, I did some research, built a meta deck within my first week, and maintained roughly a 70% win rate once I learned the ropes. Even after completing that first deck, I had nearly enough leftover wildcards to build a second one—I was only short a couple of mythics. On my current account, the game has been ridiculously generous: Massive Resource Pool: I currently have over 5,000 gold and dozens of wildcards (including over 10 mythic, 24 rare, and 50 common wildcards). That’s more than enough to craft two top-tier meta decks right now. Passive Pack Acquisition: Just by playing casually without spending cash, I’ve opened around 20 packs from the latest set. Zero Pay Pressure: I have never once felt starved for cards or pressured to open my wallet. Ironically, I’ve spent the last 30 hours playing completely unedited Starter/Standard decks. Did I lose a lot? Absolutely. But winning wasn't the goal—learning and having fun was. I haven’t even bothered crafting a new meta deck yet because I enjoy the core gameplay loop too much to rush it. I also love the crossover sets (Universes Beyond). I know that’s a divisive topic in the community, but the gameplay interactions are wild. In one match, an opponent forced me to discard my entire hand and pinged me for 5 life every time I played a card. I thought I had the win locked down when they were at 8 life, only to bleed out and lose completely. It was hilarious, unique, and easily the most fun match I’ve had in ages. How It Stacks Up Against the Competition Hearthstone Hearthstone has become an exhausting money pit. Ranked mode is overrun with bots. Card sets become irrelevant remarkably fast. Keeping up with Standard feels like it demands $150 every three months. In Magic, the 2-year Standard rotation window gives cards real longevity. Casual play easily keeps pace with the format. The disenchant/dust economy in Hearthstone is terrible. I spent hundreds of dollars on that game over the years, and after stepping away for a while, every single card I bought became useless in Standard. I returned to zero wildcards, minimal dust value, and only cosmetic items left to show for it. Combine that with high-RNG gameplay, and it simply wasn't worth staying. Yu-Gi-Oh! Yu-Gi-Oh! is actually quite welcoming and generous with its card acquisition—much like MTG. The new player experience was smooth, and getting cards for a ranked deck didn’t require cash. The problem is the modern match pacing. The game revolves heavily around One-Turn Kills (OTKs). Too many matches feel like watching someone assemble a massive solitary puzzle on turn two while you wait ten minutes to find out if you're allowed to play. It's a great game, but that specific playstyle just isn't for me. The Big Flaw: Ultrawide Support My main technical complaint is Arena’s poor Ultrawide (UWHD) implementation on PC. On a 3440×1440 ultrawide monitor, the client fails to hold its aspect ratio in fullscreen, frequently glitching or stretching when navigating between menus. I have to force a standard 16:9 window just to keep the interface stable. It isn't game-breaking, but it feels like lazy display coding for a studio this size. Final Verdict: 8/10 The game has a steep initial learning curve, optimal pack acquisition requires external research, and the PC client has technical oversights like broken ultrawide scaling. However, if you're a casual player looking for a rewarding, deep card game where you can build competitive decks without being nickel-and-dimed, MTG Arena is easily the best option on the market.

Let's talk monetization, because that is the worst part of any game like this. But the thing is, free-to-play in this game DOES NOT mean pay-to-win. You can spend stupid amounts of money on your collection if that's your thing, but you really don't need to spend a dime. Season passes? Yes, those are here, but you can actually earn the gems to unlock them through free play. You earn gold through daily quests (easily earned through starter deck duels, so you're never at a wealth disadvantage) and then you can spend that gold to enter draft competitions to win gems. The conversion rates will depend on your win rate, but you can absolutely EARN the premium currency rather than paying real money. There are more play modes than I can even count with events and opportunities constantly shifting. Some of them (constructed and historic, mainly) will be full of players with the strongest decks that money can buy, and anyone who hasn't made that kind of investment is going to lose a LOT. Still, even on your first day you'll likely have enough wildcards to build *one* such deck--but after that you'll need to pay for more wildcards or earn them very slowly before you'll have enough to build another.

title: Mycopunk
review_text: Fixes virtually every issue I have with other similar games while feeling distinctly like its own thing. Every other looter shooter I've played is very concerned about not letting the player have too much power. Not the case here. There's not a massive abundance of guns like destiny or borderlands, but there's a good variety of weapons that handle distinctly. The weapon mod system also allows you to pretty drastically alter how they feel. I also am compelled to theory craft and find new ways to break the game because (unlike destiny) the devs aren't deciding which build will be the best for the current patch. This is genuinely the first looter shooter I've played to deliver on the promise of "diablo with guns." There is many ways to make an OP character without chasing some kind of meta. It side steps a lot of the grindy feeling that other games in the genre have because it's not particularly picky about how you progress. The mission objectives are very much in the vein of something like deep rock or helldivers but the game doesn't push you too hard to play one type of mission over another. Grinding the mission chain things in deep rock just to get an unlock that felt mediocre sapped any and all energy I had to play that game after a while. The backlog system in this game allows you to give yourself that kind of structure if you crave it, but you ultimately have control over what you choose to do. You progress by getting mods for your gear and all of the activities give you mods for your gear. A thing I've come to really despise in all of these post left 4 dead co op shooters is the rigid class systems. I constantly feel like I'm being forced to give up some invaluable piece of kit in order to fit some kind of team composition. In practice if you're playing with randoms it makes it harder to step up and cover areas they may be lacking in, and it also usually makes solo play pretty miserable. This one being class based nearly put me off of it, but I actually like what they did here. The weapons are not class locked which instantly makes the whole system way more tolerable. You don't have to play the cowboy character to have a revolver. The class abilities don't fit neatly into archetypes either. You can build them to fulfill whatever type of role you want. It plays well solo too. The enemies are pretty interesting. They didn't just copy paste the specials from left 4 dead. There's definitely enemy types, but there's a lot less emphasis placed on this than you're probably used to. The enemies are modular and when you kill one the parts they dropped can be picked up and used to attack you by other enemies. I thought it was really easy for the first few missions as I was unlocking the higher difficulties, but it's not balanced around the difficulty of the individual enemies. This game has helldivers style hordes that feel very chaotic and alive when you're fighting them. The difficulty comes from trying to manage the horde. That always feels different because your objectives change depending on the mission, and the makeup of the horde its self changes as you fight it. It's really pretty unique and works extremely well with this games systems. You'll get more powerful and you will have the power fantasy/diablo style moments of making your whole screen explode, but the game never becomes a cakewalk. I don't like roguelikes, but this game also has an excellent roguelike mode. It gives you a fresh character and gives you new mods after every encounter. It gets progressively harder and there's modifiers. It's typical roguelike stuff. All of the systems the game is built on are so well put together that I actually had a ton of fun playing it though. It feels like previewing what types of builds I can make in the other parts of the game, in addition to stress testing whatever I come up with on the fly. It also gives you a way to unlock the mods that you got in the roguelike mode for your main characters, so its a really solid way to progress overall. It runs great. Art style isn't for everyone. I thought it looked kind of ugly in videos but it grew on me while I played. The music is good. Shooting things feels good. Tone is comedic, but it's pretty lightly implemented and not an overbearing assault on the senses like borderlands. There's a good hub for when you're between missions. It doesn't inundate you with tutorials. Everything feels good. I can't believe I had never heard of this prior to its full release on my steam release calendar thingy. It's also absolutely absurd that you can't find a youtube video on it from less than 10 months ago. At the time of writing there's 1 video on it from a day ago and it's AI generated. This feels like the kind of thing that should be way bigger than it is. All in all, this is the first game of it's type that doesn't feel like it's constantly trying to hold me back from the fun part. 15 bucks is generous and 7 is highway robbery. Highly recommend.

review_text: Only about halfway through the story, and I'd give this about a 6/10 at best. The sections of the game where it actually lets you stealth and infiltrate are very good and by far the only reason I've carried on so far in the story. However, both the gunplay and melee combat leave a lot to be desired. They feel clunky and worse than in the original Uncharted game, despite being extremely similar. This is a HUGE and potentially the only source of frustration. The game repeatedly forces you into using these systems rather than leaning on its strengths. I'd go so far as to say there's only been one mission so far that I would actually say is good, as it has multiple ways to get too each area, ways to disguise yourself, etc. Every other mission repeatedly relies on its weak combat mechanics. If you're a fan of stealth games and need something new, I'd say this is worth a purchase if you see it under £30. But prepare yourself to be frustrated by the combat sections, which are plentiful.
